title: Early-Start Effects in EFL Settings: A Critical Review of Long-Term Evidence Beyond the Primary School Years
abstract: This paper critically reviews long-term evidence on early English instruction in foreign language settings beyond the primary school years. It examines how early-start effects change across the transition to lower-secondary education, later school years, and college-level contexts, and which conditions are associated with their persistence, weakening, or re-emergence. Using a timeline approach, the review synthesizes school-based and post-school evidence across these stages. The findings indicate that early-start advantages are unstable, context-dependent, and often domain-specific rather than automatic or cumulative. Although cumulative exposure matters, the evidence does not support a consistent exposure threshold at which durable advantages emerge. Cross-study comparisons are also constrained by differences in assessment constructs and their alignment with program aims. Lowering the starting age alone is therefore unlikely to produce lasting benefits unless early instruction is supported by sustained, high-quality input, coherent curricular progression, careful transition planning, and meaningful opportunities to use English across educational stages.

title: Preservice English Teachers’ Emotions and Identities During Teaching Practicum: A Case Study in China
abstract: This study delves into the intricate emotional experiences of two preservice English teachers and explores how these experiences shape their evolving identities during teaching practicum. Data collection involved reflection logs, semi-structured interviews, casual communications, and tangible artifacts. Findings reveal that preservice English teachers experience a spectrum of emotions during their teaching practicum, which are shaped by primary and secondary appraisals. These emotions play a crucial role in forming, transforming, and confirming their teacher identities. Furthermore, the study shows that both participants demonstrated their agency, which was found to mediate the nexus between their emotions and their emerging identities. This research enriches the existing literature on emotions and identities in teacher education and provides valuable insights for teacher educators, mentor teachers, and policymakers.

title: AI-Informed Digital Literacy for Language Educators: Redefining Core Competencies Through TPACK and SAMR
abstract: The rapid evolution of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has transformed language education, presenting opportunities to enhance efficiency, personalisation and learner engagement. The technologies have also disrupted educators’ conventional roles, necessitating the acquisition of artificial intelligence (AI)-informed digital literacy competencies. This conceptual article explores the integration of GenAI technologies in language education through the lenses of technological pedagogical and content knowledge and substitution augmentation, modification and redefinition frameworks. By examining AI’s affordances and limitations, the article highlights the irreplaceability of the human role in cultivating critical thinking, cultural awareness, motivation and relationship-building. It calls for language educators to balance AI’s technological capabilities with pedagogical and relational expertise. Core competencies such as critical AI literacy, ethical data management and the ability to design transformative, student-centred learning experiences are essential. title: “Teaching Was Changing Me”: EFL Teacher Identity Trajectories as Dynamic Systems—An Arts-Based Narrative Inquiry
abstract: This study investigates how English as a foreign language (EFL) teachers’ role identity trajectories develop over time and how such processes are rendered visible through arts-based narrative practices. Drawing on the Dynamic Systems Model of Role Identity (DSMRI), the study adopts an arts-based narrative inquiry design with two in-service teachers in the Turkish EFL context. Data were generated through multimodal artifacts (self-portrait collages, soundtracks, literary reflections), written narratives, and post-curation meetings across a three-phase process. The analysis traced the dynamic alignment and misalignment among identity components, including beliefs, goals, self-perceptions, and perceived action possibilities. Findings revealed two predominant trajectory patterns that differed in the degree to which coherence among identity components was disrupted, maintained, and consolidated over time. The first, a perturbation-driven reorganization, was characterized by initial misalignment, contextual disruption, and subsequent cycles of reconfiguration and expansion. The second, a value-anchored consolidation, reflected a comparatively stable trajectory in which early coherence ac

title: Large Language Models for L2 Italian Writing Assessment: Effects of Prompt, Fine-Tuning, and Data Balance
abstract: This study systematically evaluates generative pre-trained transformer (GPT)-based large language models for the automated writing evaluation of Italian as a second language (L2). Drawing on 1,832 learner texts, we compare six GPT-based experimental conditions: zero-shot and few-shot prompting with GPT-4.1 and GPT-5, and two fine-tuned GPT-4.1 models trained on either class-balanced or proportionally distributed datasets. Model performance against human common European framework of reference for languages (CEFR)-based ratings is examined using exact agreement, correlation coefficients, Quadratic Weighted Kappa, precision, recall, and F1-scores. Results reveal a clear hierarchy: the balanced fine-tuned GPT-4.1 model achieves near-operational reliability, whereas all prompting-based methods, including GPT-5, remain substantially weaker. Training data balance emerges as critical, as class-imbalanced fine-tuning was associated with weaker performance on high- and low-level texts. The findings highlight the need for balanced, language-specific corpora and task-aligned fine-tuning in L2 Italian automated writing assessment.

title: Attentional Resources in Bilingual Reading: Effects of Continuous Versus Discontinuous Images on Word Memory
abstract: Studies have generally found benefits of multimodal presentation for comprehension and memory. However, although learner-related and design-related factors have received increasing attention in bilingual and L2 research, the role of visual continuity in naturalistic reading and its interaction with attentional control remains less well understood. This study investigated how the presence and continuity of visual inputs affect word recognition memory in bilingual Chinese-English university students. We also examined whether components of the attention network moderate word recognition performance. Participants read short passages in either their first language (L1) Chinese or second language (L2) English under three conditions: plain text, discontinuous images, or continuous images. Recognition memory was tested for previously seen words and semantically related foils. Results showed that the presence of images did not significantly improve recognition accuracy for previously seen words, but multimodal presentation increased susceptibility to semantic interference, regardless of language. title: The Online Effects of Processing Instruction and Structured Input on the Acquisition of the English Passive Constructions: The Role of Input Modality in Testing
abstract: This research examined both the short-term and long-term effects of processing instruction (PI) and its main element, structured input (SI), on learners’ acquisition of English passive forms. A total of 70 English as a second language (ESL) learners participated in the study and were randomly divided into three groups: a PI group ( n = 24), an SI group ( n = 25), and a control group ( n = 21). Participants in the PI and SI groups completed 1 hr of computer-based instructional activities, whereas the control group received no instructional treatment. Learners’ performance was evaluated using self-paced reading (SPR) and self-paced listening (SPL) tasks, which assessed response accuracy, picture selection response time, and reading or listening time at three points: before instruction, immediately after instruction, and after a delay. Findings showed that both the PI and SI groups achieved significant gains in accuracy on the SPR and SPL tasks at the immediate and delayed post-tests, while no improvement was observed in the control group. title: When Scripts Matter: Writing-System Effects on Metacognitive Calibration in Inferential Word Learning
abstract: Inferential vocabulary learning—deriving word meanings from context—plays a central role in vocabulary expansion, yet little is known about how writing systems shape learning outcomes and learners’ confidence in this process. This study investigated the effects of writing system on inferential vocabulary learning in learners whose first language uses the Latin alphabet. Forty-eight native Portuguese speakers learned pseudowords though incidental contextual inference. The pseudowords were presented in four scripts: Latin alphabetic, Cyrillic alphabetic, Arabic abjad, and Chinese logographic. Learning took place in either visual or auditory modality. After learning, we administered a recognition test with trial-by-trial confidence ratings. Performance was highest for Latin-based pseudowords, intermediate for Cyrillic, and lowest for Arabic and Chinese scripts, with a higher accuracy rate in the visual than auditory modality observed only for the Latin script. Difference in confidence on correct and wrong responses reflected metacognitive sensitivity, or learner’s faculty to detect those words that were less reliably learnt, and adapt confidence ratings accordingly. title: Effects of L1 Versus L2 Audio and Textual Glosses on L2 Vocabulary Learning
abstract: Although a number of studies investigated the effects of different gloss types on L2 vocabulary learning, the interaction between the language and modality of glosses remains underexplored. The present study thus examined the effects of the modality and language of glossing on L2 vocabulary learning. To this end, the study employed a within-subjects design to test the impacts of four combinations of L1 versus L2 and audio-based versus text-based glosses on L2 lexical development. The participants were 49 EFL learners who read two texts, each including 28 unfamiliar words that were the same in both texts over two sessions. They were instructed to read the texts with their smartphones and touch the target words, which were underlined to see or hear the glosses, depending on the allocation of the target words to each treatment condition. The glosses associated with the target words in the texts included L1 and L2 text-based as well as L1 and L2 audio-based glosses, equally distributed among the target words. Two testing instruments, a meaning recall task and a cued production task, were used on two occasions after the treatment sessions as post-test and delayed post-test to measure th

title: State Self-Esteem, Personal Investment, and Initial L2 Lexical Acquisition
abstract: Self-esteem is critical to learning, but it is a multifaceted construct with complex effects. The present study investigates domain-specific self-esteem in memory for novel lexis and its interaction with self-reference effects. In total, 144 Saudi learners processed novel English trait adjectives in four conditions (referenced to themselves, an intimate other, a familiar other, or synonyms). They evaluated their self-esteem at the time each item was processed and later recalled the meaning of each item (item memory) and the conditions under which they processed it (source memory). Results revealed that self-esteem had a significant impact on both item and source memory and interacted significantly with self-referential processing conditions. Participants recalled little when self-esteem was low, regardless of processing condition, but they did significantly better when self-esteem was high. Additionally, when self-esteem was high, learners recalled items processed in the personal investment conditions (with reference to themselves or an intimate other) significantly better than in the non-personal investment conditions (with reference to a familiar other or a synonym). title: Cooperative Development as a Means for Supporting Ukrainian EFL Teachers During the War
abstract: Set against the profound precarity and disruption of Ukrainian higher education during Russia’s war against Ukraine, this study examines how 9 university English as a foreign language (EFL) teachers sustained their professional lives and wellbeing through participation in a Cooperative Development (CD) initiative within a language teacher association. The study encompasses a secondary thematic analysis of transcripts from a 9-month online CD project comprising 10 structured, non-evaluative peer-support sessions in which participants alternated Speaker, Understander, and Listener roles to reflect on their professional lives through narration and dialogue. The findings showed that CD offered substantial affordances for Ukrainian EFL teachers working during wartime (regardless of their location) by facilitating emotional expression, building connectedness, and providing a safe, non-judgmental space that supported their wellbeing and promoted reflection. Participation also contributed to the development of empathetic communication, reflective skills, and confidence/motivation, although teachers initially faced challenges adapting to unfamiliar CD roles and the non-advice-giving nature

title: Investigating the Emotional Experiences in Shadow Language Education: A Mixed-Methods Study of Secondary School Students’ Enjoyment and Boredom
abstract: English private tutoring (EPT) has expanded rapidly across post-Soviet contexts, but students’ emotional experiences within this sector remain underexplored. Drawing on Control-Value Theory and positive psychology in second language acquisition, this mixed-methods study examines enjoyment, boredom and behavioural engagement among Grade 11 students attending EPT in Kazakhstan. Quantitative data were collected from 640 students across 8 tutorial centres using validated measures of emotions, engagement, learner attitudes and tutor-related practices, complemented by focus group interviews with 32 students. Results reveal that students generally reported high enjoyment, moderate engagement and low boredom. Enjoyment was associated with engagement, positive attitudes towards English, perceived competence, and tutor enthusiasm and friendliness, whereas boredom was negatively associated with engagement and with less favourable attitudes towards English and the learning environment. Tutor type also mattered, with non-Kazakhstani and highly qualified tutors associated with higher enjoyment. title: A Sociocultural Perspective for Tracing the Development of Formative Assessment Teacher Cognition: Making a Case for Transformative L2 Teacher Education
abstract: Grounded in sociocultural theory, this study examines how the formative assessment teacher cognition (FATC) of a pre-service English as a foreign language teacher developed within a teacher education context. Adopting a longitudinal single-case design, the study traces the trajectory of one focal participant, Ela, across a 10-month teaching practicum. Multiple qualitative data sources were triangulated, including interviews, reflective journals, lesson plans, classroom observations, and pre- and post-observation conferences. Data were analyzed through a hybrid approach combining reflexive thematic analysis and sociocultural discourse analysis to capture both the content and interactional dynamics of cognition-in-action. Findings indicate that Ela’s FATC evolved through two key shifts: (a) reconceptualizing corrective feedback from an evaluative and affectively risky practice to a formative tool that scaffolds learner understanding and (b) developing more explicit instructional practices that clarify learning intentions and guide student performance. These shifts reflect an emerging understanding of feedback and instruction as meaning-making processes central to formative assessment

title: Bridging Local Roots and Global Goals: Expert Teachers’ Insights on ELT Curriculum Design and Policy in Nepal’s Higher Education
abstract: The quest for inclusive and contextually relevant English Language Teaching (ELT) curricula is a priority for higher education globally. This phenomenological study examines the lived experiences of expert teachers involved in ELT curriculum design and implementation policies in Nepal. Through unstructured interviews, participants revealed dissatisfaction with top-down curriculum processes, insufficient teacher involvement, and unclear guidelines. The study underscores challenges such as curricula heavily focused on global competitiveness, limited integration of local cultures and extracurricular activities, and inadequate support for technology driven courses. Key issues include balancing cultural relevance with global competency, resource constraints, and outdated infrastructure. Findings highlight the necessity of a context driven approach, involving educators in decision-making, comprehensive needs analyses, and innovative teaching and evaluation methods. These reforms are critical for transforming ELT curricula to address local needs while preparing students for global challenges. title: Understanding Speaking Demotivation in Iranian EFL Contexts: A Self-Determination Theory Analysis of Learner and Teacher Perspectives
abstract: This study investigates how speaking demotivation is experienced and interpreted by Iranian English as a Foreign Language learners and teachers through the lens of Self-Determination Theory (SDT), with particular attention to autonomy, competence, and relatedness. Thirty participants (15 learners and 15 teachers) from two private language institutes in Iran took part in semi-structured interviews. Data were analysed using theory-informed thematic analysis. The findings indicate that speaking demotivation emerges as a contextually mediated process shaped by the interaction between learners’ psychological experiences and instructional conditions. Learners primarily emphasised affective and relational factors, including lack of social support, negative classroom climate, and limited agency, whereas teachers foregrounded structural constraints such as proficiency gaps, exam-oriented practices, and limited opportunities for authentic language use. Notable divergences between teacher and learner perspectives suggest misalignment in how demotivating experiences are recognised and addressed in classroom practice. title: From Corrective Preferences to Corrective Practice: A Critical Review of Attitudinal Studies on Oral Corrective Feedback
abstract: Studies on oral corrective feedback (OCF) have been lately tilted toward examining preferences for correction motivated by the belief that they are connected to emotional comfort, learning motivation and outcomes. Some have compared teachers’ preferences with learners’ expectations to find the mismatches between the two. Others have compared teachers’ beliefs with their practice to see how beliefs are reflected in practice. Despite the numerous studies, there seem to exist considerable gaps in the literature that merit consideration. Given the significance of studying OCF preferences, the present study presents a critical systematic review of the studies on corrective preferences to uncover the gaps. For this purpose, scientific databases, including Google Scholar, Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect and JSTOR with 16 related journals, were searched to identify the related studies in the date range of 1995 to 2025. This was to ensure inclusion of the most relevant and high-quality research studies published in well-established scientific databases and journals. title: Developing and Validating a University Language Teacher Belief Scale for AI-Assisted Instruction
abstract: Teachers’ beliefs play a critical role in shaping how AI tools are interpreted and used in instruction, yet these beliefs have rarely been systematically assessed in university language teaching. This study aims to develop and validate a measurement instrument for assessing teachers’ beliefs about AI-assisted instruction, grounded in the Intelligent-Technological Pedagogical and Content Knowledge framework. A sequential, two-wave quantitative design was employed, with data from 508 teachers used for exploratory factor analysis (EFA), followed by confirmatory validation using an independent sample of 487 teachers. Data analyses were conducted using SPSS for EFA, AMOS for confirmatory factor analysis and Mplus for measurement invariance testing. The results supported a reliable five-factor belief structure: AI knowledge beliefs, AI content beliefs, AI pedagogy beliefs, AI integration beliefs and AI ethics beliefs. The scale demonstrated satisfactory reliability, construct validity and stability. Additionally, measurement invariance results indicated that the scale functioned equivalently across gender, teaching experience and educational background. This study provides a psychometric

title: Enhancing Metacognitive Listening and Learner Autonomy Through an Artificial Intelligence-Mediated Metacognitive Listening Textbook: A Quasi-Experimental Mixed-Methods Study
abstract: Listening instruction in language education often remains product-oriented, focusing on comprehension accuracy rather than awareness of cognitive processes and learner self-regulation. Grounded in metacognitive and self-regulated learning frameworks, this study examined the effectiveness of an artificial intelligence (AI)-mediated metacognitive listening textbook designed to promote metacognitive awareness and learner autonomy through guided reflection and adaptive feedback. The textbook implemented a four-phase metacognitive cycle (planning, monitoring, evaluating, reflecting) supported by AI feedback that helped learners diagnose comprehension challenges, plan strategies, and monitor progress. A 12-week quasi-experimental mixed-methods design was conducted with 500 upper-secondary learners divided into experimental ( n = 250) and control ( n = 250) groups. The intervention comprised 24 classroom sessions featuring culturally situated informational-listening tasks aligned with learners’ communicative experiences. title: The Interplay of Task Type and Repetition in L2 Oral Performance and Attention Orientation: A Mixed-Methods Investigation
abstract: This mixed-methods study investigates how task type—independent versus integrated—and task repetition may influence the complexity, accuracy, and fluency (CAF) of second language oral performance and learners’ underlying attention orientation. Fifty-six Iranian English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners completed either an independent (reading–speaking) or integrated (reading–listening–speaking) task, repeated after one week. CAF measures captured performance changes, and stimulated recall interviews with 24 participants traced attentional allocation according to Levelt’s (1989) speech model. No interaction effects emerged, but significant main effects were found: repetition was associated with increases in syntactic complexity and accuracy, and task type affected speech rate. Stimulated recalls appeared to align with these findings, suggesting repetition redirected attention from conceptualization toward syntactic encoding, while integrated tasks created an initial attentional profile more oriented toward the Formulator. title: Pluralism Behind Boredom Coping in Language Learning: Evidence From a Q Methodology Study
abstract: The present study investigated how second or foreign language (L2) learners cope with boredom in class, using Q methodology. The participants were 40 undergraduate English majors (12 male, 28 female). By-person factor analysis identified three coping profiles, namely, acceptors , escapers , and strivers . The acceptors viewed coping as a personal responsibility and acknowledged boredom as a natural and temporary emotion. These learners reminded themselves of the value of the lesson, reflected on the causes of boredom, and planned to prepare for future situations, showing a reflective and mindful attitude. The escapers tackled boredom through mental or behavioral disengagement. They tended to distract themselves or share their feelings with peers. While they avoided confronting boredom directly, they neither blamed themselves nor the teacher. The strivers demonstrated persistence and discipline. They coped boredom by staying task-focused, taking notes, highlighting key points, and consciously redirecting attention to maintain engagement. title: Configurational Effects of Grit, Mindset, and Engagement on Language Achievement: Insights from fsQCA Approach
abstract: Second language acquisition is a lengthy and complex process fraught with numerous obstacles and barriers. It requires learners to possess robust grit, adaptive mindsets, and active engagement to overcome the challenges encountered during the learning process. However, limited antecedent research has integrated the three factors into one framework and examined the configured joint effects on language achievement outcomes. Adopting a fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA), 431 tertiary-level university students were recruited to complete grit, engagement, and mindset questionnaires, and their language achievement was assessed through the grades they attained on the College English Test Band 4. The results from the direct path analysis and fsQCA analysis led to two major findings. First, perseverance of effort and behavioral engagement positively, albeit weakly, predicted L2 achievement, while fixed mindset negatively predicted achievement. Second, grit, mindset, and engagement can be configured in distinct ways that collectively contribute to high L2 achievement. title: Dynamic Changes in Pre-Service Language Teacher Well-Being in Practicum: An Ecological Approach
abstract: Responding to calls for more complex dynamic systems theory (CDST)-oriented and ecological studies on teacher well-being, this study investigates the role of practicum in the well-being of pre-service English language teachers (PELTs) in a Turkish English-as-a-foreign-language context. Designed as a case study and grounded in CDST and ecological systems theory, it examines how well-being unfolded within the Turkish practicum setting. Data were collected from two PELTs through self-ratings at 5-min intervals over three teaching sessions, supplemented by semi-structured interviews and reflective journals. Findings underscore the dynamic nature of well-being within the practicum ecology: it fluctuated positively in response to student engagement, successful task completion, and clear communication, and negatively due to challenging tasks, comprehension difficulties, and time pressure. Moreover, analysis of systemic factors across micro, meso, exo, macro, and chrono levels revealed a range of ecological influences on well-being, including the ecologies of interactions, (mis)alignment, educational institutions, societal expectations, and teacher career trajectories. title: Motivational Trajectories of Chinese Secondary School EFL Learners: Understanding Demotivation and Remotivation Through a Bioecological Lens
abstract: This study drew on bioecological systems theory to investigate factors influencing demotivation and remotivation among Chinese secondary school EFL learners. Adopting a sequential explanatory mixed-methods design, 129 Grade-12 students were asked to create motivational change graphs to depict their English learning trajectories during their 12-year pre-tertiary education. Analysis of the graphs revealed two distinct groups: those who remained demotivated and those who experienced remotivation. To explore underlying factors, narrative frames and follow-up interviews were conducted with selected participants. Quantitative results indicated two critical periods of motivational change: Grade 8, when both groups experienced their first visible decline, and Grade 12, when the remotivation group experienced a dramatic recovery while the demotivation group underwent a sharper decline. title: Interrupting the Loop: EFL Teacher–Learner (De)motivation During Critical Incidents
abstract: Motivation in language classrooms is often treated as an individual trait, yet periods of disruption reveal how strongly it is shaped through interaction. This study examines how learner and teacher (de)motivation was experienced and enacted during the return to offline English as a foreign language instruction following pandemic-related disruption. Using a convergent mixed-methods design, data were collected from learner and teacher questionnaires, regression analyses, Motivational Identity System-informed domain mapping, and teacher observational accounts. Findings indicate that learners maintained interest in English learning while experiencing moderate cognitive–emotional demotivational strain, suggesting vulnerability rather than pervasive demotivation. In contrast, teachers reported cumulative demotivational pressure arising from institutional conditions, classroom interaction, and pandemic-related constraints. Integrating these perspectives reveals a teacher-observed, interactionally mediated (de)motivational loop at the point where internal learner experience and classroom interaction intersect, in which teachers’ interpretations of learner responsiveness shaped instruction

title: Stylistic Alignment and Sentiment in L1–L1 and L2–L2 English Task-Based Dialogues
abstract: Dialogue constitutes a primary context in which interlocutors coordinate their language use through the interplay of cognitive and social factors. Stylistic alignment refers to the convergence of interlocutors’ language styles during interaction, facilitating communicative coordination and fostering rapport. However, the extent to which cognitive and social factors jointly influence stylistic alignment in naturalistic dialogue remains insufficiently understood. To address this gap, the present study examined how cognitive and social factors are associated with stylistic alignment in L1–L1 and L2–L2 dialogues. Stylistic alignment between interlocutors was assessed using language style matching (LSM) metrics across multiple linguistic features, and a social affective factor, operationalized as text sentiment, was evaluated using a BERT-based sentiment analyzer. Results indicated that both L1 and L2 speakers demonstrated robust stylistic alignment across most linguistic features, with alignment strength varying by feature. title: Effects of xu -Based Continuation Writing on the Longitudinal Development of L2 Productive Vocabulary Knowledge
abstract: Productive vocabulary is widely recognized as an essential component of second language proficiency, yet it remains one of the most challenging aspects of lexical development. This study investigated whether continuation writing could enhance learners’ productive vocabulary knowledge. In a longitudinal experiment, 75 Chinese EFL learners were assigned to either an experimental group or a control group. The experimental group completed a continuation writing practice every 2 weeks, followed by a free writing post-test 1 week later; the control group completed independent writing practices and took the same post-tests. A total of 525 essays were collected. Indices of lexical density, diversity, and sophistication were extracted using TAALED and TAALES, and analyzed through linear mixed-effects models and repeated-measures correlation analyses. Results showed that while both task types improved learners’ lexical density and diversity, continuation writing had distinct advantages in promoting lexical sophistication. title: Exploring EFL Learners’ Pre-Class Textbook Use and Web-Based Peer Learning: A Qualitative Case Study
abstract: Web-based peer learning (WPL) is widely recognized as effectively complementing students’ learning activities. However, its role in students’ textbook use, which is an important aspect of students’ knowledge construction, is still unknown, particularly with respect to pre-class textbook use. To fill this knowledge gap, this qualitative case study explored WPL’s role in pre-class textbook use (i.e., textbooks used before in-class instruction of a new text) of 15 students enrolled in an English-as-a-foreign-language reading course at a university in China. A thematic analysis of multiple data resources (e.g., interviews with students and students’ web-based activities) collected over a semester was conducted. The results showed that in addition to improving their reading literacy, the students’ WPL helped them retain the content learned from their pre-class textbook use, contributing to their continued motivation for consuming and re-consuming new texts. WPL also helped the students gain an in-depth, comprehensive understanding of the text, overcoming individual knowledge limitations. title: Learning to Teach Across Borders: Vietnamese Pre-Service TESOL Teachers in a Transnational Practicum in Thailand
abstract: Practicum is an integral part of initial teacher education, functioning as a bridge between theory and practice. In today’s globalized context, practicums have extended beyond national boundaries into transnational settings. This study examined the experiences of 12 Vietnamese pre-service TESOL teachers during their transnational practicum at a university in Thailand. Data were collected through four focus group interviews (pre-practicum and post-practicum) with the pre-service teachers. Findings reveal that the practicum catalyzed professional development and intercultural learning. Participants encountered tensions between theory and practice as well as imagination and reality, but addressed these through contextual adaptation and pedagogical flexibility. Their transnational experiences also contributed to the initial shaping of their language teacher identity. The paper concludes with implications for research and practice in the design and implementation of transnational practicums in second language teacher education.

title: The Relationship Between Writing Strategies and Writing Performance in Story Continuation Writing Tasks
abstract: This study examined the components of writing strategies employed in the story continuation writing task (SCWT) and investigated how these strategies related to different aspects of writing performance. Specifically, it adopted factor analyses to validate the strategy subscale of Ye et al.’s (2021) writing performance questionnaire and used structural equation modeling (SEM) to explore the relationship between strategy use and writing performance, as measured by the holistic writing scores and 11 textual indices. The data comprised 330 questionnaire responses and 330 SCWT essays produced by the same group of high school English as a Foreign Language learners selected through convenience sampling. Factor analyses identified three task-specific strategy components: reading_to_select , reading_to_organize , and content_developing . These components represent learners’ alignment with the reading passage at the linguistic, discoursal, and situational levels and correspond to the processes of imitation, extension, and creation as conceptualized in the xu -argument. title: On the Effects of Spaced Versus Massed Practice on Deliberate Learning of English Idioms across L2 Proficiency Levels
abstract: This study investigated the effects of spaced versus massed practice on the deliberate learning of English opaque idioms across different second language (L2) proficiency levels. A total of 199 Iranian EFL learners at different proficiency levels were taught 40 opaque idioms under either spaced (distributed over 5 days) or massed (concentrated in two sessions) conditions. Learning outcomes were measured through immediate, short-delayed (12 days), and long-delayed (100 days) cued-form and meaning-recall posttests. Results showed that while massed practice led to better immediate recall for the low-proficiency learners, spaced practice resulted in superior long-term retention for mid- and high-proficiency learners. These findings underscore proficiency as a critical boundary condition of the spacing effect within a memory-scheduling framework, suggesting that while massed practice supports initial encoding for learners with limited L2 resources, spaced practice facilitates durable retention for those with established proficiency. The study findings extend spacing effect to multiword expressions and offer pedagogical insights into adaptive vocabulary instruction tailored to learner pr

title: Notes on Contributors
Correlation, Mediation, and Causation: Methodological Reflections on Current L2 Research
Enhancing EFL Oral Proficiency through Video-Based Tasks Implemented in a Flipped Classroom
abstract: This study investigates patterns associated with the integration of video-based tasks within a flipped classroom model grounded in task-based language teaching (TBLT) in relation to English as a foreign language (EFL) learners’ speaking fluency, accuracy, and engagement. TBLT emphasizes meaning-focused, real-world tasks that encourage authentic communication and learner autonomy. The study involved 50 Indonesian university students enrolled in an advanced speaking course. Over 6 weeks, participants engaged with TED Talk videos outside the classroom and completed structured in-class speaking tasks aligned with TBLT principles. Quantitative findings showed observable differences between pre- and post-participation assessments, with gains in fluency (+1.56) and accuracy (+1.36) based on CEFR-aligned assessments and paired-sample t -tests ( p r = 0.81) than behavioral engagement. Qualitative data from classroom observations and student reflections frequently referred to greater confidence, more spontaneous interaction, and evidence of self-monitoring during speaking activities. title: Profiles of EFL Emotion Regulation Strategies and Associations With Regulatory Emotional Self-Efficacy and Burnout
abstract: Although second language (L2) emotions have been intensively investigated in the recent decade, little attention has been paid to how L2 learners regulate their L2 learning emotions. It also remains unknown how different combinations of emotion regulation strategies (ERS) relate to learners’ regulatory emotional self-efficacy (RESE) beliefs and L2 burnout. The current study recruited 777 Chinese undergraduates of English as a foreign language (EFL) by administering a battery of questionnaires. Latent profile analysis indicated that three distinct groups of learners emerged, namely the Adaptive Group (40.5%), the High ERS Group (6.8%), and the Maladaptive Group (52.7%). Three-step Bolck–Croon–Hagenaars (BCH) analysis revealed distinct group differences in RESE and burnout. The Maladaptive Group reported the lowest levels on both RESE dimensions, indicating weaker confidence in managing emotions. The Adaptive Group demonstrated the highest level of RESE in expressing positive emotions (RESE-POS), while the High ERS Group showed the highest level of RESE in regulating negative emotions (RESE-NEG). Regarding burnout, the Adaptive Group consistently reported the lowest levels of emotion

title: Learning Motivation and Academic Satisfaction Among Spanish College Students Learning Chinese as a Foreign Language: An Empirical Analysis
abstract: Higher education serves as a fundamental driver of social progress and individual professional development. This study examines the motivational profiles of 112 Spanish-speaking college students who are learning Chinese as a foreign language, focusing on the factors that influence their decision to study this language and their academic satisfaction within the university context. The study is based on an analysis of data collected from these students, using statistical analyses to explore relationships between motivational factors, academic satisfaction, and academic performance. The findings reveal that intrinsic motivations—such as interest in Chinese culture and traditions, personal growth, and intellectual challenge—predominate over extrinsic motivations, including prospective employment opportunities, when selecting Chinese as a foreign language as a major or compulsory subject. In addition, both intrinsic and extrinsic motivations show distinct associations with specific dimensions of academic satisfaction. The statistical analyses further indicate that there is a positive correlation between motivation, academic satisfaction, and academic performance, as measured by grade po

title: Navigating Neoliberal Demands: Linguistic Entrepreneurship Among EMI Students in a Non-Elite Chinese University
abstract: English-medium instruction (EMI) has rapidly expanded in Chinese higher education, yet its implementation often lacks a solid research foundation and overlooks the politico-economic dimensions of education. This article reports on a case study of how EMI students from a second-tier Chinese university, an under-investigated population, navigated and internalized neoliberal values. Using the framework of linguistic entrepreneurship and data from semi-structured interviews, classroom observations, and institutional documents, the study revealed that students perceived EMI as a means to overcome their disadvantages and enhance their competitiveness in China’s stratified educational market. However, insufficient English proficiency led to unexpected learning challenges and often prompted them to adopt grade-oriented strategies that circumvented or undermined meaningful learning. These findings highlight the frequent tensions between neoliberal expectations and educational realities. The article concludes with policy and practical recommendations to mitigate the influence of neoliberal ideologies amid nationwide hyper-competition in China.

title: Engagement and Efficiency: A Study of Metadiscourse in Tibetan EFL Classrooms
abstract: This study investigates the use of metadiscourse in Tibetan English as a foreign language (EFL) classrooms, drawing on Activity Theory to examine the sociocultural and institutional factors shaping teachers’ discourse. Using a mixed-methods approach, it combines quantitative analysis of metadiscourse patterns with qualitative insights from interviews and classroom observations. Findings reveal an overall low frequency of metadiscourse, with a dominant use of interactional metadiscourse and meta-talk, particularly topic-shifting, student-inclusive pronouns, self-mention, and attitude markers. In contrast, interactive metadiscourse, particularly expert, paraphrase, and example markers, was notably scarce, suggesting limited scaffolding for textual coherence or deeper meaning negotiation. This pattern reflects a teacher talk style prioritizing efficiency, authority, and engagement, shaped by policy pressures, exam-oriented objectives, limited instructional time, and routinized pedagogical practices. Interpreted through Activity Theory, the findings highlight how teachers’ metadiscursive choices are influenced by tensions between curricular ideals and systematic constraints. While teac

title: Relationship Between Pre-Writing Task Perception and Post-Writing Feedback Handling: The Mediating Role of During-Writing Task Implementation Strategies and Moderating Role of Second Language Writing Proficiency
abstract: Second/foreign language writing consists of a cycle of three phases (i.e., forethought, performance, and reflection) that interact with each other. However, studies on the interaction of these different phases are limited. Self-regulated strategies are used and enacted differently across these phases of second/foreign language writing, forming sequential relationships within the strategic system. However, the interconnections among phase-specific strategies (especially the theoretically directional relationships across these three phases) remain underexplored. Combining structural equation modeling and thematic analysis, this study explored the impact of pre-writing task perception on post-writing feedback handling, with five during-writing task implementation strategies as mediators and second/foreign language writing proficiency as a potential moderator. Analyses of 336 surveys and 14 interviews collected from Chinese second-year university English learners revealed three major findings. First, pre-writing task perception significantly and positively predicted post-writing feedback handling, but students’ English writing proficiency did not significantly moderate this relationshi

title: Effects of Experience and Foreign-Accented Input on L1 Ecuadorian Spanish Speakers’ Production of English Vowels
abstract: This study examined the impact of experience and foreign-accented input on the production of second language (L2) English vowels by Spanish-speaking adult learners in a formal instructional language environment. The participants were first language (L1) Ecuadorian-Spanish speakers enrolled in an English program at a state university in Ecuador. Twenty-four third-level and 22 eighth-level learners completed a monosyllabic isolated word production task in English with the following vowels: /i ɪ ɛ æ ʊ u ɑ ʌ/. The same procedure was also conducted with their Ecuadorian English teachers. The tokens were acoustically analyzed, and the Mahalanobis distances between the pairs /i ɪ/, /ɛ æ/, /u ʊ/, and /ɑ ʌ/ were calculated using F1, F2, and duration values. The results were not uniform for all pairs of vowels, with the high pairs /i ɪ/ and /u ʊ/ displaying significant distances for the teachers, but not for the learners, and the /ɑ ʌ/ being significantly distant only for one group of teachers. The low-front pair /ɛ æ/ was the only one with significant distances for all groups. Interestingly, the inclusion of one bilingual teacher with near-native pronunciation increased the distinctiveness

title: Culturally Adaptive Teaching in One-to-One Live Online Chinese Language Instruction: A Cross-Cultural Study of Learner Engagement and Learning Outcomes
abstract: This study investigates whether culturally adaptive teaching strategies (CATS) enhance instructional effectiveness in one-to-one online Chinese language teaching. Drawing on a controlled experimental design, 177 learners from South Korea ( n = 42), Japan ( n = 38), Vietnam ( n = 32), the United States ( n = 28), and several European countries ( n = 37) were randomly assigned into either an experimental or a control group. The experimental group received eight culture-specific interaction protocols embedded within one-to-one teacher–learner interactions, while the control group followed the platform’s standard instructional script. Instructional effectiveness was assessed through both classroom interaction and learning outcomes. Classroom interaction was analysed through systematic coding of lesson recordings, focusing on learners’ production of unsolicited questions, follow-up probes, and uptake of structured feedback. Learning outcomes were assessed using pre- and post-course proficiency tests. Results showed that across all countries, learners exposed to CATS demonstrated significantly higher levels of real-time engagement, producing more unsolicited questions and follow-up probe

title: The Use of Indirect Positive Evidence in Second Language Morphological Learning by Different First Language Learners
abstract: This study investigates the impact of learners’ first language on their detection of indirect positive evidence presented in their second language while learning the plural morphology of an additional foreign language. The goal is to explore an alternative approach to learning foreign language grammars. The participants were 43 native Thai-speaking and 42 native Spanish-speaking learners of Mandarin who had advanced proficiency in second language English. They were divided into experimental and control groups and learned 12 Mandarin nouns in their singular form over 2 consecutive days. Only the experimental group was exposed to indirect positive evidence that provided evidence of the unmarked plural feature in Mandarin. After the learning phase, participants’ knowledge of the learned words was tested using singular and plural prompts. Follow-up questions were asked to investigate the basis of participants’ responses. The results showed that six Thai and three Spanish participants detected and used the indirect positive evidence. This finding suggests that language learners differ in their ability to adopt and use indirect positive evidence as a function of their first language back

title: Exploring the Relationship Between Online Learning and Face-to-Face Communicative Competence: A Case of English-as-a-Foreign-Language Students in Vietnam
abstract: This study investigates the relationship between online learning and face-to-face communicative competence among students of English as a foreign language in Vietnam. Drawing on the Community of Inquiry framework and Spitzberg and Cupach’s Model of Interpersonal Communication Competence, the study employed a mixed-methods design to examine students’ perceptions of online learning and the relationship between online learning frequency and speaking performance. Quantitative data were collected from 161 English-major students through a questionnaire measuring online learning exposure and engagement and a performance-based speaking test assessing face-to-face communicative competence. Correlation analyses were conducted to examine the relationship between online learning frequency and speaking performance, followed by semi-structured interviews to further explore students’ learning experiences. The findings indicate that students generally reported positive perceptions of online learning, particularly regarding accessibility, flexibility, and learning convenience. However, a high frequency of online learning was associated with poorer students’ speaking performance. Qualitative finding

title: Classroom Relationship Profiles: Links with English-as-a-Foreign-Language Students’ Academic and Social Goals and Self-Regulated Learning Strategy Use
abstract: Classroom relationships represent a complex and dynamic system, in which students’ relationships with teachers and peers are intertwined with each other. A person-centered approach was used to investigate how multiple characteristics of a good-quality relationship (i.e., validation, caring, and instrumental guidance) with teachers and peers combined to form English-as-a-foreign-language primary school students’ classroom relationships profiles. Four distinct profiles of classroom relationships were identified: Supportive, Teacher-oriented, Moderate, and Isolated. Whether students’ gender and English proficiency level significntly predicted their likelihood of belonging to each profile was tested. The profiles were analyzed to see if there was a link to academic and social achievement goals and self-regulated learning in English language learning. The results indicated that the students in the Supportive and Teacher-oriented profiles were more likely to have a higher English proficiency who adopted achievement goals and used self-regulated learning strategies more frequently than those in the Moderate and Isolated profiles in English learning.

title: The Effectiveness of Multilingual Versus Monolingual Approaches to L2 Teaching and Learning: A Meta-Analysis of Learning Outcomes
abstract: The debate on multilingual (codeswitching) versus monolingual (immersive, target-language only) approaches to second language (L2) teaching has received renewed attention in recent decades. Both approaches are employed in L2 teaching and learning, supported by competing philosophies regarding the need for maximal L2 input and the facilitative potential of first language (L1) inclusion. Given a growth in experimental research comparing the effectiveness in terms of learning outcomes of the two approaches in L2 classrooms, this meta-analysis study investigates the effects of multilingual versus monolingual approaches on outcomes as measured by language assessments and examines the variables (age, proficiency, learning context, target skill area, and procedure for learning) that moderate such effects. We conducted a comprehensive search for empirical investigations of the topic, resulting in 24 studies comprising 30 samples with a total of 2,138 learners after the application of inclusion and exclusion criteria. Through aggregating the effect sizes from this sample, analyses revealed that compared with a monolingual approach, a multilingual approach better facilitated L2 learning with

title: When Teacher Enthusiasm Meets Student Engagement: The Reciprocal Role of Perceived Learning Value in the Second Language Classroom
abstract: Second language (L2) classroom is a dynamic and evolving space shaped by ongoing interactions between teachers and students. Understanding how these dynamic interactions unfold from a psychological perspective is critical for advancing L2 learning and teaching. This study contributes to this endeavour by examining the reciprocal relationship between teacher enthusiasm and L2 student classroom engagement as well as the mediating role of perceived learning value in this reciprocal relationship. Data were collected from 317 English as a foreign language learners in Vietnam at three time points across an academic semester and analysed by means of random-intercept cross-lagged panel modelling. Results revealed that teacher enthusiasm and L2 student engagement were reciprocally related over time, and this reciprocity was mediated by students’ perceived value of L2 learning tasks. These mediated reciprocal relations remained robust even after controlling for prior levels of each construct. The findings highlight the co-regulated and cyclical nature of L2 classroom affective-motivational climate and offer practical implications for L2 pedagogy.

title: Approaches to Boost Foreign Language Learners’ Positive Emotions: A Qualitative Study on Learners’ and Teachers’ Perspectives in the Modern Foreign Language Context in England
abstract: This study builds on insights into the crucial role learner emotions play in their flourishing. It investigates learners’ and teachers’ perspectives on how to enhance positive emotions both inside and outside modern foreign language classrooms in England, amidst a language crisis and reduced modern foreign language uptake across the United Kingdom. A thematic qualitative text analysis of 18 semi-structured interviews with secondary-level teachers and learners from 7 schools across England revealed that both learners and teachers emphasise the significant impact of teachers on fostering positive emotions in the classroom. They also showed that students lack awareness of the benefits of learning languages beyond English. Furthermore, the interview data suggests that the government, schools, school leaders, and parents must also engage to elevate the status of modern foreign languages and promote positive social change.

title: The Activity Design Typology: A Practitioner-Centered Approach to Understanding Task Structure
abstract: As the central construct in task-based language teaching (TBLT), “task” has been defined in a myriad of ways. Though popular criterion-based definitions offer a tantalizingly straightforward description of the construct, they have, at times, proved difficult to apply in practitioner contexts. With over 17 definitions identified in the literature, prominent scholars have advocated for efforts that offer a more unified understanding of “task” that may be better able to support task-based language teaching in implementation initiatives. This exploratory, qualitative study examines how two cohorts of K–16 U.S.-based world language teachers ( n = 35) approached task design in a task-based teacher education program from a materials development perspective. An analysis of the 114 activities teachers created revealed that although submissions had task characteristics, the intricacies of their designs were not adequately captured by traditional task criterion. Subsequent analysis following a directed content approach identified five distinct categories of activity design. Advancing previous interest in expanding the binary distinction of “task” versus “non-task,” we drew on these categories

title: AI-Assisted Digital Storytelling in EFL Teacher Education: A Qualitative Case Study of Digital and Multimodal Literacy Development
abstract: This qualitative case study explores how English as a foreign language (EFL) student teachers engaged with generative artificial intelligence (GAI) in the collaborative design of digital stories within an advanced undergraduate course in 2024. During the semester, participants critically evaluated and applied various AI applications, such as text-to-image generators, automated video editors and speech synthesis tools, to support different stages of multimodal story production, including script drafting, visual design, audio narration and video editing. Drawing on a corpus of 69 reflective papers (approximately 75,000 words), the study examines how student teachers integrated visual, auditory and textual elements to achieve multimodal cohesion and narrative coherence. The analysis focuses on participants’ practices and strategies for aligning modes, maintaining consistency across media, and adapting to the constraints of AI-generated content. Findings indicate that the project’s primary pedagogical significance lay not in technical efficiency but in the productive ‘friction’ generated by algorithmic limitations, which led participants to move beyond passive tool use and become criti

title: Motivation Through Extensive Reading: A Self-Determination Theory Perspective on Young Learners of English as a Foreign Language
abstract: This study investigates the impact of an extensive reading program on the English learning motivation of young middle-school learners of English as a foreign language, utilizing the self-determination theory framework. Eighty-one Grade 7 students participated in a semester-long extensive reading program designed to provide supportive conditions by allowing students to select reading materials that matched their proficiency levels and personal interests. Employing a mixed-methods approach, quantitative data were collected through pre- and post-motivation questionnaires measuring intrinsic motivation, external regulation, introjected regulation, and identified regulation, whereas qualitative data were obtained from student interviews and teacher focus groups. This study identified a multi-factor structure of motivation. It also revealed a significant increase in overall motivation, with intrinsic motivation, identified regulation, introjection regulation, and external regulation notably enhanced. Qualitative findings identified key factors contributing to motivational changes, including heightened interest in English classes, English subject, and English language; a greater sense of

title: The Effect of Text Shadowing on English Language Learners’ Pronunciation Development: A Quasi-Experimental Study
abstract: Shadowing is a technique that has been shown to significantly improve English language learners’ (ELLs) oral fluency and comprehensibility. However, previous research showing dramatic gains over time for ELLs has varied in design, with some studies including control groups and others not, thus complicating interpretations of efficacy. These studies have also been conducted in English and other languages with attention to advanced-level ELLs and beginning-level ELLs. Additional research is needed to provide insight into the effect of shadowing on intermediate learners, as well as using treatment and control groups to get a more accurate picture of identified changes in fluency, comprehensibility, accentedness, and imitative ability. A ten-week quasi-experimental study of text shadowing practice was conducted with intermediate-level adult ELLs studying in a large western university’s intensive English program (IEP). Speech samples from the pretest and posttest were rated by non-expert native English-speaking raters for fluency, comprehensibility, accentedness, and the quality of imitative speech on nine-point Likert scales, as has been used in other pronunciation studies. title: When Does it Really Matter? Exploring the Conditions under which Gestures Affect Students’ Language Recall, Pronunciation Accuracy, and Cognitive Load in the EFL classroom
abstract: Gestures are widely recognized as an integral aspect of multimodal communication and language learning. However, the conditions under which they effectively support learning remain unclear. This study investigated when gesture matters in English as a foreign language (EFL) learning through three controlled experiments. Experiment 1 (3 × 2 design) examined the effects of gesture type (iconic, deictic, metaphoric) and production mode (human tutor vs. virtual agent). Experiment 2 compared gesture engagement (watch vs. imitate), while Experiment 3 tested gesture timing (synchronous, gesture-first, misaligned). University-level EFL learners participated in 30-minute instructional sessions, with outcomes measured in language recall, pronunciation accuracy, and cognitive load using multivariate analysis of covariance. Results showed that gesture enhances learning selectively rather than uniformly. Higher recall and pronunciation accuracy were observed when gestures were iconic, actively imitated, and temporally aligned with speech. Misaligned gestures increased cognitive load and reduced performance. Differences between human tutors and virtual agents were present but modest. These findin

title: Not the Artificial Intelligence, but the Sequence: Instructional Design and Oral Communication Strategy Development
abstract: This study examines how instructional design shapes the development of oral communication strategies in an 18-week English-as-a-foreign-language speaking course, at a time when generative artificial intelligence is often assumed to enhance speaking performance. All three classes worked with the same curriculum and speaking tasks. One class learned through a BOPPPS (Bridge-In, Objective, Pre-Assessment, Participatory Learning, Post-Assessment, and Summary) based sequence in which students prepared ideas, participated in guided speaking activities, and reviewed their performance, with each cycle including a stage where they generated their own content before using ChatGPT to refine it. A second class received regular teacher guidance and completed the same tasks, but their use of ChatGPT was self-directed and not part of a fixed sequence (the artificial intelligence-flex condition). A third class covered the same material through teacher-supported face-to-face interaction without artificial intelligence (the traditional condition). Learners completed the Oral Communication Strategy Inventory at the beginning and end of the semester and provided reflections on how their course format

title: Transforming Traditional Translation Training: The Role of Policy, Practice, and Institutional Support in Student Skill Enhancement
abstract: Globalization has revolutionized translation training, and English education policies have encouraged more practical, innovative, and, in this regard, oriented teaching approaches. This study investigates the multi-level effects of English education policies on translation training at the national (macro), institutional (meso), and classroom (micro) levels, with particular attention to how policy influences the adoption of innovative instructional models and students’ perceived learning-related outcomes. Using a mixed-methods design, qualitative data were gathered through semi-structured interviews with 78 respondents, including policymakers, administrators, instructors, and students, whereas quantitative data were collected through a survey of 436 translation students (undergraduate and postgraduate). Qualitative data were analyzed using NVivo, and SPSS and SmartPLS were used to analyze quantitative data. The results indicate that translation training (β = .373, p p

title: Comparing Teacher and Artificial Intelligence Scoring in Writing Assessment: A Generalizability Theory Analysis
abstract: This study examined the use of artificial intelligence tools, which have garnered significant attention in recent years, in the assessment and evaluation processes of language education. For this purpose, student essays were scored by Turkish middle school teachers and artificial intelligence tools both with and without the use of a rubric, and the findings were evaluated based on generalizability theory. Additionally, the research findings were shared with participants to gather qualitative data, which were analysed using the inductive thematic analysis method to support the research results. The findings revealed that in evaluations conducted without a rubric, teachers were limited in their ability to distinguish individual differences and demonstrated low scoring consistency. In contrast, artificial intelligence tools were more effective in distinguishing individual differences and exhibited high consistency. In evaluations conducted using a rubric, scoring consistency increased in both groups, although, as in the first evaluation, artificial intelligence tools demonstrated a higher level of consistency. title: Instructional Practices for Signed Literacy: Observations of 38 Deaf Education Classrooms
abstract: This mixed-methods study examined how signed literacy instruction is currently taught in United States deaf education classrooms (PreK-3) and to what extent that instruction reflects evidence-based composing instruction. Signed literacy instruction means teaching students to view, analyze, and compose texts in a signed language. A composing-forward approach treats students’ production of signed texts as the central instructional activity, with language skills taught in service of that composition. This approach is the core of Strategic and Interactive Signing Instruction (SISI), a pedagogical framework for signed literacy. Participants were 38 teachers across 11 deaf education programs. Each teacher completed a survey on their instructional practices and was observed teaching lessons selected to demonstrate support for deaf children’s signing skills. Survey and observation data were analyzed separately, then compared for agreement, complementarity, and divergence. Nine of 38 teachers included signed composition in their observed instruction. Of those 9, only 6 (16% of the full sample) met the evidence-based composing instruction threshold. These 6 teachers consistently treated sign

title: Exploring Teacher Agency in Conducting Peer Feedback Activities in English-as-a-Foreign-Language Writing: An Ecological Perspective
abstract: Although the learning benefits of peer feedback in English-as-a-foreign-language writing instruction have been well recognized, the process and effects of peer feedback are largely reliant on teacher agency in conducting such activities. However, inadequate research has been conducted on this issue, leaving the dynamic features and causes of teacher agency in peer feedback largely unknown. Drawing on an ecological perspective, this comparative case study examined how two English-as-a-foreign-language teachers from two universities enacted agency in organizing peer feedback activities in their writing instructions. Multiple data including classroom observation, interviews and relevant teaching documents were collected and coded for themes. The study revealed that both teachers exerted dynamic agency in creating peer feedback experiences for students, but showed considerable differences before, during and after peer feedback. Overall, the novice teacher shifted from showing proactive agency to constrained agency, whereas the experienced teacher moved from demonstrating automatic agency to autonomous agency. This stark contrast was shaped by the synergism of different temporal afforda

title: Enhancing English-as-a-Foreign-Language Speaking Performance through Self-Regulated Strategy Instruction: Evidence from Chinese University Learners
abstract: The present study investigated the effects of self-regulated strategy-based speaking instruction on English-as-a-foreign-language learners’ speaking performance and strategy use. Despite extensive research on self-regulated learning in various educational contexts, its application to second language speaking development remains underexplored. This explanatory mixed-methods quasi-experimental study employed self-report questionnaires, speaking assessments, and semi-structured interviews for data collection. A linear mixed-effects model results revealed that the experimental group ( n = 54, receiving the self-regulated learning strategy-based intervention) demonstrated significantly greater improvement in speaking performance compared to the control group ( n = 53, receiving traditional instruction), with effects sustained at delayed post-testing. Quantitative analyses further indicated significant increases in participants’ use of self-regulated learning strategies. Qualitative findings corroborated these results, revealing more frequent, deliberate, and sophisticated strategy application among intervention participants. Interview data also suggested differential intervention effect

title: Outcome-Based Language Teaching in EMI Listening: Balancing Accountability With Ungraded Supports for Low-Proficiency Learners
abstract: Listening plays a critical yet undertheorized role in English-medium instruction (EMI), where subject courses are taught through English rather than learners’ first language, and access to disciplinary knowledge relies heavily on real-time comprehension of lectures and academic tasks not designed for language development. For low-proficiency students enrolled in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) programmes, this creates a high-stakes learning condition in which assessment-driven accountability can intensify cognitive and affective pressure. While outcome-based education (OBE) offers curricular structure and transparency, it is frequently criticized for privileging measurable outcomes over sustained engagement and long-term skill development. This study examines how accountability in EMI listening courses can be structurally balanced with ungraded pedagogical supports to foster engagement and learning sustainability. Drawing on a three-year longitudinal reform of a compulsory elective EMI listening course, the study analyses how a design approach integrating graded accountability with collaborative learning, voluntary practice, and reflective work reshaped lea

title: Embarking on Virtual Exchange for English as a Multilingua Franca Context: Comparing Virtual Reality and Non-Virtual Reality Approaches to Enhance Second Language Speaking Fluency
abstract: Many learners of English as a foreign language struggle to develop second language speaking fluency because of limited opportunities for authentic communication with linguistically diverse English users in English as a multilingua franca context. This study aims to address this problem by investigating the effects of communication strategy instruction, an approach believed to facilitate communication in English as a multilingua franca contexts. This study compared two approaches of communication strategy instruction, explicit and implicit, combined with low-immersion virtual reality. Over 11 weeks, 159 Vietnamese undergraduates were randomly assigned to one of three instructional conditions: Explicit + virtual reality, Explicit + non-virtual reality, and virtual reality Implicit. Data sources were video recordings of pre-, post-, and delayed speaking tests, as well as learners’ reflections. The data were analyzed using the ELSA Speech Analyzer to measure second language speaking fluency and qualitative content analysis to explore learners’ perceived affordances and challenges of virtual reality implementation. title: The Production Effect in Second Language Verb–Noun Idiom Learning: Evidence From Pure-List Designs and Transfer-Appropriate Processing
abstract: Learners of a second language often vocalize newly learned items, and previous studies have shown that this practice facilitates the learning of single words and multiword expressions. However, these effects have been demonstrated only in mixed-list designs, where a single list of items is learned using multiple learning methods, and have not been tested in pure-list designs, where each list is learned with one consistent method. Moreover, prior research has relied almost exclusively on written recognition tests, leaving spoken-modality tests and recall measures largely unexamined. This study employed a within-participant, pure-list design in which each list was associated with a single learning condition, and each participant studied a total of four lists. The participants were 68 Japanese learners of English. Participants learned 64 verb–noun idioms assigned across four active learning conditions (Listening, Repeating, Reading while Listening, and Reading while Repeating), with 16 items in a fifth condition serving as a no-exposure Control condition. title: Understanding Chinese English-as-a-Foreign-Language Learners’ Self-Regulated Learning: Insights from Q Methodology
abstract: From a social cognitive perspective, self-regulated learning is essentially and increasingly recognized as a complex and dynamic experience. The use of self-regulated learning strategies is also inherently subjective, shaped by individuals’ experiences, beliefs, learning styles, and environmental influences. Although existing research has explored self-regulated learning via a complex dynamic system theory lens, relevant studies that depart from a learner’s point of view and elucidate complexity and subjectivity in their understanding of self-regulated learning strategy use remain limited. Researching the complexity of self-regulated learning in second language acquisition aids in fostering a supportive and inclusive language learning environment. Hence, this study aimed to identify, depict, and compare divergent opinions regarding self-regulated learning strategy use among Chinese English-as-a-foreign-language learners using Q methodology and semi-structured interviews. Thirty learners of English as a foreign language participated in Q-sorting, ranking 50 self-regulated learning-related statements on a grid from “-4” (strongly disagree) to “+4” (strongly agree). The data were anal

title: The Role of Autonomy-Supportive Teaching in Academic Achievement and Learning Anxiety: Evidence From Teaching Turkish as a Foreign Language
abstract: This study aims to examine the effect of instructors’ behaviors supporting learner autonomy on students’ academic achievement and anxiety levels related to reading, listening, writing, and speaking skills in teaching Turkish as a foreign language. The study was conducted during the 2023–24 academic year with two sample groups, consisting of 1,002 students learning Turkish and 115 instructors working at the School of Foreign Languages of a state university. Participants were selected using simple random sampling within the accessible population. Reliability and validity analyses of the scales were conducted, and the adequacy of the measurement models was confirmed through confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) and the Heterotrait–Monotrait Ratio (HTMT). According to the results of multiple group analysis and canonical correlation analysis, the necessity (β = 0.114, p p = 0.001) dimensions of learner autonomy support behaviors had a positive and significant effect on academic achievement. However, the effect of foreign language learning anxiety on academic achievement was not statistically significant (β = −0.031, p > 0.05). title: Gamified Language Learning: The Impact of Role-Playing Games on Beginner Japanese Acquisition
abstract: This study examined the effectiveness of Nihongo Quest, a theory-driven role-playing game (RPG) developed for beginner learners of Japanese. Sixty undergraduate students participated in an eight-week quasi-experimental study comparing a game-based learning (GBL) condition with a traditional textbook-based condition. Results indicated that participants in the GBL group demonstrated significantly greater gains in vocabulary ( d = 1.45) and grammar ( d = 1.05) than those in the textbook group. In addition, the GBL group reported higher levels of intrinsic motivation ( η ² = .25) and lower levels of language learning anxiety ( η ² = .16). These outcomes are attributed to the game’s systematic alignment with core second language acquisition (SLA) frameworks, including the input–interaction–output (IIO), self-determination theory (SDT), willingness to communicate (WTC), and sociocultural theory (SCT). Through the integration of multimodal literacy tasks, interactive dialogues, and culturally situated scenarios, Nihongo Quest reduced cognitive load while supporting both linguistic and pragmatic development.
